name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning framework maintained by the Keras team, first released in 2015 and now at version 3.0. It provides high-level building blocks for neural networks and runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO. A reader deciding whether to use it should know that Keras 3 lets one codebase target multiple backends, though performance varies by model and backend.

sections.body: Keras is an open-source deep learning framework written in Python and maintained by the Keras team, with its source hosted at github.com/keras-team/keras under the Apache-2.0 licence. The project describes itself as deep learning for humans, and its official site is keras.io. It first appeared in 2015 and reached version 3.0, announced on the official site, which introduced multi-backend support. Keras sits at the high-level API layer of the AI stack. It provides layers, models, metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, training and evaluation loops, and saving and serialization infrastructure. Rather than executing tensor operations itself, Keras 3 runs on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO for inference-only, so it serves as the model definition and training interface above those computational engines.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras covers the concrete jobs of deep learning work: training, evaluation, inference, data preprocessing, and model saving. The official guides show image classification with MNIST, autoencoders built with the functional API, transfer learning for flower classification, and text generation with a scaled-down GPT model built using KerasHub. Built-in methods such as fit(), evaluate(), and predict() handle training and inference loops, and the site states these work the same way across Sequential models, functional API models, and subclassed models. Keras is strongest when a developer wants readable, concise model code that can move between backends. The Keras 3 page notes that any model using only built-in layers works immediately with all supported backends, and that existing tf.keras models using built-in layers can run in JAX and PyTorch right away. It is also a reasonable choice for transfer learning and for prototyping architectures quickly, as the sample size estimation example demonstrates with a pre-trained ImageNet backbone.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed as a high-level API, and the official site presents it through guided examples that start from loading a dataset and building a small model. The Sequential guide shows that a model can be created by passing a list of layers, and that layers generally need to know their input shape before weights are created. The functional API guide introduces more flexible model construction with named inputs and outputs. A beginner needs basic Python and some familiarity with NumPy arrays, since the guides pass NumPy arrays or tf.data.Dataset objects to training loops. The site does not present formal prerequisites in mathematics or systems programming, and it does not state a required level of calculus or linear algebra. What it offers a beginner is a large set of runnable guides and examples, including complete training runs with printed accuracy and loss values, which makes the first working model relatively quick to reach.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras has a substantial ecosystem. The Keras 3 page states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. The framework implements over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, and saving infrastructure. The keras.ops namespace provides operations such as ops.matmul, ops.sum, ops.stack, ops.einsum, ops.softmax, ops.binary_crossentropy, and ops.conv that work across backends. KerasHub supports model building with components such as TokenAndPositionEmbedding and TransformerDecoder layers. The repository has 64,354 stars on GitHub and showed a last push on 2026-10-06. The official site provides guides, examples, and API documentation, and the Keras 3 distribution API, keras.distribution, is currently implemented for the JAX backend with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, though the trade-offs differ by backend. The Sequential and functional APIs make it fast to define and train a model, and the built-in fit() and evaluate() loops remove boilerplate. For production, Keras 3 offers backend choice: the official page states that in benchmarks JAX typically delivers the best training and inference performance on GPU, TPU, and CPU, but results vary from model to model, and non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function. The distribution API supports model parallelism, data parallelism, and combinations of both, currently on the JAX backend. The cost of this flexibility is that performance is not uniform, and the site does not claim a single backend is always fastest.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The official Keras 3 page states that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. The repository has 64,354 stars, and the project is actively maintained, with a last push recorded on 2026-10-06. These facts indicate that Keras is a current standard rather than a legacy choice, and that experience with it is relevant to production AI work. The site does not provide detailed hiring data, salary information, or a breakdown of which industries use Keras most. For someone choosing what to learn, the supported facts point to a widely used framework with multi-backend reach, but the official material does not quantify job market demand beyond the developer count and the named systems.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is written in Python and is typically used alongside the backends it supports: JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, and OpenVINO for inference-only. The Keras 3 page describes it as usable as a low-level cross-framework language to develop custom components such as layers, models, or metrics that can be used in native workflows in JAX, TensorFlow, or PyTorch with one codebase. The fit(), evaluate(), and predict() routines accept tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, NumPy arrays, and Pandas dataframes regardless of backend. This places Keras in a polyglot pattern where the model definition and training logic stay in Keras while the execution engine and data pipeline can come from another framework. The site states that as long as only ops from keras.ops are used, custom layers work with JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow with the same code.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The official material is clear about some limits. The Sequential model is not appropriate for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, and the functional API is recommended instead. The distribution API is currently implemented only for the JAX backend, with TensorFlow and PyTorch support described as coming soon, so multi-backend distribution is not yet complete. Benchmark performance varies by model and backend, and the site does not promise that one backend is always fastest. The site does not state minimum hardware requirements, does not give a full comparison against other high-level frameworks, and does not detail the maturity of every backend feature. It also does not say how long the TensorFlow and PyTorch distribution implementations will take to arrive, or what limitations exist for OpenVINO beyond inference-only use.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
